## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle components can approach the streaming ceiling on death-free workloads.

## Cache saturation
All measured N (≥4000) sit past the L1d spill at N≈963, so the L1d transition is not directly observed. From N=4000 to N=16000, cost FALLS sharply at every death rate (7.729→5.27 ns/p at q=0.01; 10.745→7.892 at q=0.25), reflecting fixed-overhead amortization at small N. Crossing the L2 spill at N≈61680 (between N=16000 and N=65000) produces no knee: cost stays FLAT (5.27→5.128 at q=0.01; 5.902→5.83 at q=0.05). From N=65000 to N=4000000 cost continues a slow FLAT-to-declining drift (5.128→4.897 at q=0.01). Death rate raises the floor without reshaping the N-curve: the post-16000 plateau lifts from ~4.9 ns/p (q=0.01) to ~5.7 (q=0.05), ~6.2 (q=0.1), and ~7.9 (q=0.25). At q=0.5 the curve goes entirely flat at ~27.3 ns/p even at N=4000, meaning respawn overhead saturates from the smallest N.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 13.89 GB/s at N=4000000, q=0.01 — 55% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling. The algo is bandwidth-limited but ceiling-remote at low churn, holding 11–14 GB/s (44–55% of ceiling) for q≤0.1 across all large N. Death rate drives the transition: q=0.25 falls to 8.57 GB/s (34%), and q=0.5 collapses to 2.49 GB/s (9.9%), shifting the regime from bandwidth-bound to overhead-bound. The bandwidth never approaches the ceiling at any measured death rate or N.

## Assembly
The compiler vectorized component-wise within a single particle, not across particles. The update loop issues `ldr q1, [x25]` to load four floats, then `fmul.4s v0, v3, v4` and `fadd.4s v0, v1, v0` to update position in one 4-wide lane, followed by `fmul.2s`/`fadd.2s` for a two-component velocity update. A gather is present: `ld1.s {v2}[1], [x8]` performs an indexed single-element load into one vector lane from address x8=x25+0x14. The render loop uses `uqadd.8b` for saturating byte adds but then scatters through 19 `strb` and 13 `ldrb` instructions with per-pixel `csel` clamping. This byte-granular scatter, combined with the per-particle (not per-lane) vectorization granularity on stride-68 data, explains why bandwidth plateaus at 55% of ceiling rather than streaming.

## Verdict
Refuted — at the lowest measured death rate (q=0.01) the algo sustains only 13.89 GB/s = 55% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling, and the component-wise vectorization (`fmul.4s` on single-particle data, `ld1.s` gather, 19 `strb` scatter stores) cannot stream at line rate. Death rate worsens the picture: q=0.5 collapses to 2.49 GB/s (9.9% of ceiling) under branchy-respawn overhead. The hypothesis that auto-vectorization approaches the streaming ceiling does not hold in any measured regime.
